title: Entitlement to benefits (anti-abuse)
summary: Article 29 carries the BEPS Action 6 minimum standard against treaty abuse. It has three parts: a limitation-on-benefits (LOB) rule in paragraphs 1 to 7, in simplified and detailed versions; a rule for income routed through PEs in low-tax third States (paragraph 8); and the principal purposes test, or PPT (paragraph 9), which denies a benefit where obtaining it was one of the principal purposes of an arrangement, unless granting it would be in line with the treaty's object and purpose.
readingNote: For Saudi treaties the PPT is the part that matters. Saudi Arabia implements the minimum standard through the preamble and the PPT, by adopting MLI Articles 6 and 7(1) without a limitation-on-benefits rule, and newer Saudi treaties include a PPT article directly. The LOB guidance below is condensed because it rarely applies to Saudi treaties. See the KSA view tab for which treaties the MLI changes.

entries.t: The Article reflects the preamble's intention not to create opportunities for non-taxation or reduced taxation through evasion or avoidance, including treaty shopping. States can meet the minimum standard in three ways: the PPT alone, the PPT plus an LOB rule (simplified or detailed), or a detailed LOB plus rules against conduit arrangements.

Combining a general rule (the PPT) with specific objective tests (LOB) gives both flexibility and certainty. Some States, such as those with strong judicial doctrines, may prefer the LOB route with separate anti-conduit rules instead of the PPT.

Paragraphs 1 to 7 deny benefits to structures that typically pass treaty benefits indirectly to third-State residents. The tests look at the resident's legal nature, ownership and activities to confirm a sufficient link with its State of residence.
The Article restricts the other provisions of the Convention, including Article 1. Benefits under Articles 4(3), 9(2) and 25 are not denied by paragraph 1.

Paragraph 1: a resident gets treaty benefits only if it is a 'qualified person' under paragraph 2, or meets one of the other tests in paragraphs 3 to 6. The rule applies whenever a benefit is claimed and does not extend any benefit.

Paragraph 2 lists qualified persons. The tests are self-executing, without needing a competent-authority ruling. Individuals and the Contracting States, with their political subdivisions, local authorities, agencies and instrumentalities, qualify.

Publicly traded companies qualify if their principal class of shares is regularly traded on a recognised stock exchange. The detailed version adds a primary-trading or management-and-control requirement, tested throughout the taxable period.

Detailed version: subsidiaries of publicly traded companies qualify if owned at least 50 per cent by up to five such companies, subject to a base-erosion test. Worked examples and optional variations, such as on special tax regimes, are given.
Certain non-profit organisations and recognised pension funds qualify, with rules for funds of funds.

Ownership and base-erosion test: an entity qualifies if at least 50 per cent is owned by qualified residents and, in the detailed version, less than 50 per cent of its gross income is paid as deductible payments to ineligible persons. Examples follow.
Collective investment vehicles: whether and how to give them benefits depends on the States' analysis of treaty-shopping risk, with several drafting options linked to the Commentary on Article 1.

Paragraph 3, active conduct of a business: a non-qualified resident still gets benefits for income that emanates from, or is incidental to, an active business in its residence State. Holding, group financing and investment activities do not count. Income from connected persons requires a 'substantial' residence-State business, and connected persons' activities can be attributed. Examples follow.

Paragraph 4, derivative benefits: an entity owned mainly (95 per cent in the detailed version) by 'equivalent beneficiaries', who would get the same or better benefits directly, qualifies subject to a base-erosion test. Drafting options are given.

Paragraph 5 (detailed version only): headquarters companies of multinational groups can qualify for dividends and interest if they meet six conditions on management, geographic spread and base erosion.

Discretionary relief: a competent authority may grant benefits to a person failing the tests if establishing, acquiring or maintaining the person, and conducting its operations, did not have obtaining treaty benefits as one of its principal purposes. Requests should be handled quickly, and States may set procedures to discourage vexatious requests.

Definitions: recognised stock exchange, shares, principal class of shares, dual listed companies, connected person, equivalent beneficiary (with detailed rate-comparison rules and examples), disproportionate class of shares, primary place of management and control, qualifying intermediate owner, tested group, gross income, and collective investment vehicle.
Simplified version: the competent authorities may agree how the paragraphs are applied.

sections.heading: Paragraph 8: income attributable to PEs in third States

entries.t: Shares, debt-claims or rights can be moved to PEs in third States that do not tax, or lightly tax, the income from them. Where the residence State exempts the profits of such PEs, the source State should not be expected to grant treaty benefits on that income, unless the income bears a significant level of tax where the PE is, or comes from an active business there.
The taxpayer may ask State S's competent authority to grant benefits anyway, if justified given the reasons the requirements were not met.

Example: a company routes income through a PE in a low-tax third State. The rule covers all types of income, not only business profits. Benefits are denied where the third-State tax is less than the lower of a bilaterally agreed minimum rate applied to the income and 60 per cent of the tax the residence State would have charged if the PE were located there. The source State may then tax under its domestic law.
'The amount of that item of income' means the net amount after the relevant expenses, so the tax comparison is made on comparable bases.
The exception for income that emanates from, or is incidental to, an active business is read in the same way as the active-business test in paragraphs 74 to 76.
Some States may prefer a wider rule covering other situations where a PE in any State, including the source State, is low-taxed. Alternative wording is offered.

The PPT reflects the guidance on improper use in the Commentary on Article 1. A benefit is denied if one of the principal purposes of an arrangement or transaction was to obtain it, unless granting it would be in accordance with the object and purpose of the relevant provisions.
The PPT supplements, and is not limited by, the LOB and paragraph 8. Qualifying under the LOB does not prevent denial under the PPT.

The PPT must be read in the context of the whole Convention and its preamble. A listed company that qualifies under the LOB is not denied benefits merely because of who its shareholders are, but it can be denied them for an unrelated abusive transaction, such as a bank's conduit financing arrangement for a third-State resident.
Benefits can be denied where it is reasonable to conclude, considering all the relevant facts and circumstances, that obtaining them was one of the principal purposes.

'Benefit' covers every limitation on source taxation in Articles 6 to 22 (reduced rates, exemptions, deferrals, refunds), relief under Article 23, protection under Article 24, and any similar limitation such as tax sparing.

'Directly or indirectly' is deliberately broad: the abusive transaction need not be the one generating the income. Example: transferring an existing loan to a treaty-resident subsidiary to obtain an interest exemption.
'Arrangement or transaction' is read broadly. It covers any agreement, understanding, scheme or series of transactions, enforceable or not, including steps such as setting up or acquiring a person.

Purpose requires an objective analysis of all persons' aims and the circumstances, case by case. Conclusive proof of intent is not needed, but treaty purpose should not be lightly assumed, and looking at effects alone is usually insufficient. An arrangement that can only reasonably be explained by a treaty benefit points to a principal purpose.
Merely asserting a commercial purpose is not enough. All the evidence is weighed.
Obtaining the benefit need not be the sole or dominant purpose. It is enough that it is one of the principal purposes.

Arrangements inextricably linked to a core commercial activity, whose form was not driven by tax benefits, are unlikely to have such a principal purpose. Seeking similar benefits under many treaties does not reduce the purpose for any one treaty, and domestic-law motives do not make the treaty benefit merely incidental.

Thirteen examples. Benefits denied: A, assigning dividend rights to a treaty resident; B, a usufruct over preferred shares to get the 5 per cent rate; J, splitting a construction contract to stay under the PE threshold. Benefits not denied: C, a factory location chosen for commercial reasons; D, a widely held investment vehicle's portfolio; E, raising a holding from 24 to 25 per cent after the treaty enters into force; F, buying a company for business expansion; G, a regional company with real functions; H, group financing and treasury functions; I, collective music-rights management; K, a regulated investor's regional investment platform with substance; L, a widely held securitisation company; M, a real estate fund's holding company.
States whose domestic general anti-abuse rule needs senior approval may agree a similar process for the PPT.

Optional paragraph: where the PPT denies a benefit, the competent authority may still grant that benefit or a different one, if it would have been available without the arrangement, after consulting the other State. Example: the 15 per cent portfolio rate granted after the 5 per cent rate is denied for an abusive assignment of dividend rights.
States that do not accept the PPT need anti-conduit rules or doctrines alongside the detailed LOB. Examples show what is and is not a conduit arrangement.

membersNote: Paragraph 188 is an observation (United States) and paragraphs 189 to 192 are reservations on the Article. Non-OECD economies' positions are in section P(29). Those relevant to your treaty appear in the Other countries tab.
